items.title: OptiCover: A Scalable and Multi-Surface Framework for Cold-Start Visual Optimization under Semantic Constraints
items.summary: Selecting an effective cover photo is a critical yet understudied problem in visual merchandising for e-commerce marketplaces. On Airbnb, hosts upload many photos depicting different rooms, amenities, and points of interest, but must manually choose a single static cover photo that is reused across heterogeneous product surfaces. This creates substantial challenges: over 90\% of listing photos have no engagement labels, leading to a severe cold-start regime; guest preferences vary across surfaces and search intents, and visually captivating photos may be semantically misaligned with the underlying listing. At Airbnb scale, this corresponds to hundreds of millions of photos and hundreds of thousands of new uploads per day. We propose \emph{OptiCover}, a scalable framework for cold-start visual optimization under semantic constraints and multi-surface engagement signals. The framework combines (i) a photo candidate generator that identifies candidate photos through various proxies, (ii) lightweight vision heads applied to frozen CLIP embeddings for large-scale semantic scoring, (iii) a cross-modal grounding validator based on a vision-language model (VLM) that enforces semantic representativeness, and (iv) an Exploration Logging Module (ELM) that orchestrates the collection of randomized engagement data across heterogeneous product surfaces and contextual search intents. We evaluate OptiCover through extensive offline studies and multiple online experiments across HomePage, and Search surfaces. OptiCover is now deployed in production and performs tens of millions of photo swaps daily. Online results show a 1.5\% engagement lift on the HomePage and a 0.35\% increase in bookers on Search, generating millions of dollars in incremental revenue. Our findings suggest that action-space shaping and semantic constraints are primary drivers of performance.

items.title: Memory-Efficient Active Perception for Embodied Question Answering in Dynamic Human-Populated Scenes
items.summary: Embodied Question Answering (EQA) couples active visual perception, vision-language reasoning, and sequential decision making, and has traditionally been evaluated in temporally stable environments where visual evidence can be accumulated reliably. In realistic multimedia settings such as dynamic human-populated scenes, however, moving people and transient occlusions introduce human-induced perceptual variations: task-relevant multimodal cues become transient, viewpoint-dependent, and incompletely captured in individual views. Conventional store-then-retrieve strategies generate redundant visual evidence and incur high inference cost, making them ill-suited to such variations. This exposes two core problems for embodied agents: resolving viewpoint-dependent ambiguity, and maintaining compact evidence for efficient inference. To address these challenges, we present DIVRR (Dynamic-Informed View Refinement with Relevance-guided Rotation and adaptive memory selection), a training-free active evidence-acquisition framework for EQA. DIVRR combines question-conditioned room guidance with relevance-triggered view augmentation to guide exploration and additional observation. Selective memory admission uses the same relevance signal as view augmentation to retain high-scoring evidence, reducing stored entries while keeping the retrieved visual context compact. To evaluate EQA under human-induced perceptual variations, we introduce DynHuman-EQA, a dynamic human-populated EQA dataset constructed in Habitat, comprising dynamic and static subsets under shared scene layouts. Experiments on DynHuman-EQA and HM-EQA show that DIVRR outperforms existing baselines in both accuracy and memory efficiency. The gains are most pronounced in dynamic human-populated scenes.

items.title: SNAPRAG: Cost-Efficient Knowledge Extraction Attack on RAG Systems via Adversarial Perturbations
items.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems improve Large Language Model (LLM) responses by incorporating information from external knowledge bases. However, recent studies have shown that attackers can extract substantial portions of private knowledge bases from RAG systems through repeated querying. Yet, state-of-the-art extraction attacks either rely heavily on external LLMs to generate adversarial queries or require a large number of queries. In this paper, we propose SNAPRAG, a novel and cost-efficient attack for extracting RAG knowledge bases through adversarial perturbations. Our approach algorithmically generates adversarial queries without relying on external LLMs and allows for a strictly configurable query budget. In particular, SNAPRAG uses a discrete token-mutation algorithm to generate novel queries in a strict black-box setting. Our adaptive dissimilarity threshold calibration systematically forces queries into unexplored semantic regions of the target database, enabling extraction with fewer queries. Specifically, to extract half of the target knowledge base, our method requires up to 6.77$\times$ fewer queries than existing approaches. Furthermore, within a fixed query budget, our method recovers up to 96.9%, outperforming the closest approach by 7.7-19.9%. We further evaluate SNAPRAG against active defenses, where it remains the leading attack on four of five defended targets, achieving 50.7-96.3% extraction rate.

items.title: It is becoming f*cking dangerous: one command in Claude Code turns your codebase into a map, 141K stars in 7 months
items.summary:
It is becoming f*cking dangerous: one command in Claude Code turns your codebase into a map, 141K stars in 7 months

1. Install with uv, the package has two y's: uv tool install --python 3.13 graphifyy

2. Add the skill to Claude Code: graphify install

3. List tests, docs and images in .graphifyignore: test factories took 6 of the top 10 spots in a repo Graphify reviewed, each image gets its own subagent

4. In a repo you trust, start Claude Code at the root, type /graphify . (tree-sitter parses code with no LLM, Claude still spends tokens running it)

5. Open graphify-out/graph.html and read GRAPH_REPORT.md: most connected nodes first, then surprising connections

6. Ask with words from your code: graphify query "auth token", or trace a path: graphify path "A" "B" --undirected

7. Remind Claude to check the graph: graphify claude install, rebuild the code part on every commit: graphify hook install

Every edge is tagged EXTRACTED, INFERRED or AMBIGUOUS: check the source before you trust the last two

It introduces a dedicated legal framework for artificial intelligence (AI), adopts a risk-based approach to regulation, and places fundamental rights considerations at the heart of compliance. [...] Ultimately, while the EU AI Act introduces a novel regulatory framework for AI, businesses that already understand post-market monitoring, incident reporting, corrective action and regulatory engagement may be better placed than they expect to respond to its requirements. The challenge is likely to lie not in the underlying governance disciplines themselves, but in applying them to a new category of risks, including those relating to fundamental rights. [...] In that sense, the EU AI Act expands the categories of harms that must be monitored and managed. This means that, while many of the governance mechanisms found in the EU AI Act resemble those found elsewhere in product regulation, the nature of the risks that need to be assessed is considerably broader.

items.title: The EU AI Act has entered the real world: What organizations need to do now | perspective | SC Media
items.summary:
COMMENTARY: The EU AI Act entered into force on Aug. 1, 2024. Two years later, on Aug. 2, 2026, its broader application phase began, with several obligations already active and others scheduled for later stages.

More importantly, the European Commission’s AI Office and national competent authorities now have enforcement powers for provisions applicable at this stage.

items.title: First Harmonised Technical Standard Published Under the EU AI Act
items.summary: The AI Act follows the EU New Legislative Framework (NLF) approach to product regulation. 1 Legislation establishes essential requirements for products, while harmonised European standards provide the technical details that support compliance with them. Some address the technical conformity of products, others organisational processes such as quality management. [...] Under the AI Act, essential requirements for high-risk AI systems are set out in Chapter III, Section 2 (Articles 8-15) of the Act. Providers must ensure that their high-risk AI systems comply with these requirements before their systems are placed on the market in the EU. [...] On 14 October 2026, the European Commission published the first harmonised standard under the EU AI Act: EN 18286:2026 – Artificial intelligence – Quality management system (Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274). Compliance with this standard can be relied upon by providers of high-risk AI systems to demonstrate compliance with Articles 11(1) (Technical Documentation) and 17(1) (Quality Management System) of the AI Act.

items.summary:
CP Asymmetry in τ→Kπν τ within Non-Minimal SU (5)
Gaber Faisel∗
Department of Physics, Faculty of Arts and Sciences,
S¨ uleyman Demirel University, Isparta, Turkey 32260.
S. Khalil†
Center for Fundamental Physics,
Zewail City of Science and Technology,
6th of October City, Giza 12578, Egypt.
Direct CP asymmetry in semi-leptonic τ decays is an intriguing hint for new physics beyond the
standard model. We investigate the CP asymmetry in τ−→K 0 Sπ−ντ andτ−→K−π0ντ decays in
non-minimal SU(5) model, with 45-dimensional Higgs multiplet. We show that the associate color-
triplet scalar is a natural example of a scalar leptoquark that mediates the transition τ→s¯uντ, and
accounts for the 2.8 σ discrepancy between the ACP(τ−→K 0 Sπ−ντ) experimental results and the
SM expectation. Furthermore, it predicts a sizable ACP(τ−→K−π0ντ), of order O(10−3), which
can be accessible in current and near future experiments.
I. INTRODUCTION
Semi-leptonicτ decays are very interesting venue for investigating Physics Beyond the Standard Model (BSM). The
CP asymmetry of τ→ K0 Sπντ is an example of an observation that points to new physics. The Belle collaboration
reported evidence for CP violation in the τ→ KSπν decay mode in 2011 [1], which the BaBar collaborations later
conﬁrmed [2]. It was the ﬁrst time to observe CP violation in a purely leptonic decay process. The observation of
direct CP violation in the τ→K0 Sπν decay has sparked further research into physics BSM. According to the result
reported by BaBar collaborations, the CP asymmetry in τ−→K0 Sπ−ντ decay is given by [2].
ACP(τ +→K0 Sπ+ντ) = Γ(τ +→K0 Sπ+ντ)− Γ(τ−→K0 Sπ−ντ) Γ(τ−→K0 Sπ−ντ)− Γ(τ +→K0 Sπ+ντ)
=−(3.6± 2.3± 1.1)× 10−3. (1)
According to the Standard Model (SM) this process occurs via τ−→ s¯uντ transition and no direct CP violation
signal is expected. However due to the CP violation in K0− ¯K0 mixing at one loop level, the SM expectation of
ACP(τ +→K0 Sπ+ντ) is of order 2×Re(εK), and the total signal should be [3–6]
ACP(τ +→K0 Sπ+ντ)|SM = (3.32± 0.06)× 10−3. (2)

† skhalil@zewailcity.edu.eg

2
Therefore, there is a 2.8 sigma discrepancy that may indicate the presence of direct CP violation, which is absent in
the SM. The presence of new sources of CP violation beyond the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix in BSM
can contribute to theτ→K0 Sπν decay’s direct CP asymmetry. These contributions could result from new interactions
involving particles not found in the standard model, such as charged Higgs boson, new particles in supersymmetric
extensions of the SM or the scalar leptoquark.
The decay τ−→ K−π0ντ has also been investigated experimentally, with a branching ratio of order 2 .7× 10−3
[7]. There have been attempts to measure the direct CP asymmetry of this decay, motivated by observations of CP
violation in the τ−→K0 Sπ−ντ decay channel. However, no reported results have been provided so far. Because these
two processes are correlated, we will predict the direct CP asymmetry in the K− channel associated with accounting
for the 2.8 discrepancy in K0 S channel, by the new physics CP violation eﬀect.
Non-vanishing direct CP asymmetry requires an interference between two contributed amplitudes with non-
vanishing weak and strong relative phases. If the total amplitude is given by A1eiδs 1eiδw 1 +A2eiδs 2eiδw 2 , then the CP
asymmetry is given by
ACP =−4|A1||A2| sinδs sinδw, (3)
where δs = δs 1−δs 2 and δw = δw 1 −δw 2 . Both K− and K0 S channels occur on quark level in the SM via the tree
level transition τ→s¯uντ, so their amplitudes are essentially real. After going beyond the tree level, the SM predicts
negligibly direct CP asymmetry of order 10 −12 [8]. Previous studies of CP violation in this decay channel has been
conducted in supersymmetric extension of the SM [9, 10], multi Higgs models with complex couplings [11] and eﬀective
models with scalar leptoquarks [11]. These studies demonstrated that the estimated direct CP asymmetry is so small
that further research is warranted.
The scalar leptoquark is one of the best candidates for mediating this decay at the tree level. It contributes to the
amplitude with scalar and tensor operators that have non-vanishing strong and CP weak phases that diﬀer from the
SM CKM phase. Furthermore, leptoquark is naturally predicted in GUT extensions of the SM. One version of the
SU (5) GUT model includes 45 (adjoint) Higgs ﬁelds [12]. This model is known as the ”non-minimal SO(5). The
adjoint Higgs ﬁeld contributes toSU (5) breaking down to the SM gauge group and provides a good ﬁt to the observed
particle masses and mixing angles, thereby resolving one major problem with the minimal SU (5). The color-triplet
scalar is one of the components of the 45 Higgs, which can be as light as TeV if ﬁne tuning similar to the well-known
doublet-triplet splitting in GUT models is considered [13]. It is worth noting that because it has no coupling with
quark-quark [14], this triplet does not contribute to proton decay.
In this paper, we consider the above-mentioned SU (5) color- triplet scalar, which is a natural example of scalar
leptoquark. This type of leptoquark diﬀers from the general adhoc examples of leptoquarks discussed in the literature.
As previously stated, it interacts in a speciﬁc way, so it does not contribute to proton decay but does contribute to
τ→s¯uν decay. We emphasize that this contribution can account for the observed direct CP asymmetry in τ→Kπν
decay.
The paper is structured as follows. Section 2 provides a brief overview of the CP Asymmetry in τ → Kπν
decay within the SM and beyond. Section 3 is devoted to discussing the SU (5) scalar leptoquark and its associated
interactions, emphasizing that while it does not contribute to proton decay, it can play a signiﬁcant role in the decays
under consideration. The analysis of the new contribution of our scalar leptoquark to direct CP asymmetries of the

decay modes τ−→ K0 Sπ−ν and τ−→ K−π0ν is discussed in section 4. Finally our conclusions and prospects are
give in section 5.
